A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with readable text, equations, figures and complete appendices. The original appendices can be matched across versions; v1's Appendix J becomes Appendix M in v2, which adds Appendices J-L.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulations of transition thresholds, Lyapunov spectra and attractor dimensionality, including noise and simulation-parameter robustness experiments in the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original simulations and adds empirical studies of quenched transition-point variability, weight pruning and delayed-memory XOR performance.

M1.justification: Appendix L introduces a limited reservoir-computing adaptation: a linear readout produces delayed-XOR predictions from the recurrent dynamics. The alpha-stable weight construction, tanh recurrent update, annealed approximation and QR-based Lyapunov algorithm remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix L adds delayed-memory XOR with structured binary stimuli separated by silent delays. This substantially extends coverage from autonomous and Gaussian-noise-driven dynamics to a computational task requiring memory and nonlinear binary prediction.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the retained experiments is unchanged. Gaussian networks remain the reference, and the new XOR experiment extends the existing heavy-tailed-versus-Gaussian comparison. The pruning variants are ablations; newly cited papers are not evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds controlled removal of the weakest 95% or strongest 1% and 3% of weights in N=1000 networks, plus delayed-XOR evaluation using test accuracy across gain values. These introduce substantial new experimental procedures and a task-performance metric. Settings for the retained experiments are unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendix J examines how quenched transition-point distributions scale with network size. Appendix K tests whether extreme synapses drive the slow transition and reduced dimensionality by comparing strong- and weak-weight pruning. These add distinct statistical and mechanistic analyses beyond the retained noise, initialization and simulation-duration checks.

E5.justification: Figure 17 introduces estimates based on 100 independent weight matrices, with three independently seeded estimates per network size, and reports mean, standard deviation and coefficient of variation. This adds a distribution-estimation procedure; it does not establish increased replication of the retained experiments.

E6.justification: Figures 1-16 retain their results. New Figures 17-21 report that annealed theory underestimates the mean quenched threshold, pruning extreme weights removes the slow transition and changes dimensionality, and heavy-tailed reservoirs sustain high XOR accuracy across a broader gain range. These are substantial added findings, not improvements to previously reported same-setting scores.

T1.justification: Appendix B corrects Equation (20) by inserting the missing factor s: the leading term changes from 1 - A_alpha(B_alpha - ln s) to 1 - A_alpha s(B_alpha - ln s). This restores consistency with the subsequent derivation. The main transition formula and logarithmic scaling conclusion remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The introduction extends the robustness contribution to claim improved information processing, supported by superior performance on a simple reservoir-computing task. v1 discussed computational benefits as implications or future work. The central finite-size transition and robustness-dimensionality tradeoff claims remain intact.

C2.justification: v2 adds an extreme-synapse explanation for robustness and low dimensionality, a hypothesis connecting Lyapunov-spectrum dispersion to weight heterogeneity, and activation-dependent applicability limits. Appendix J also identifies annealed underestimation and suggests weak self-averaging. These substantially expand the mechanism discussion and qualifications.

D1.justification: The new appendices specify absolute-magnitude pruning rules and fractions, network size, and the binary-stimulus/linear-readout setup. Existing hardware, dependency versions and code-access information are retained in Appendix M, formerly J. XOR delay lengths, dataset sizes and readout-fitting details are not supplied.

R1.justification: v2 adds Cornford et al. on exponentiated-gradient learning, Jin et al. on cell types, Wiseman and Domany on self-averaging, and Huh and Sejnowski as task precedent. These provide limited additional positioning and context; the relationship to the principal prior heavy-tailed-network studies is retained.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence remain intact. v2 makes localized wording and citation-style edits, adds explanatory paragraphs and acknowledgements, updates author/contact and conference text, and inserts Appendices J-L before the renamed implementation appendix.

P2.justification: Five new multipanel figures substantially expand the visual evidence: transition-point statistics, three pruning comparisons and paired dynamics/XOR-performance plots. Existing Figures 1-16 and the software table retain their content, with some relocation through page reflow.

improvement.justification: The new scaling and pruning analyses strengthen support for finite-size behavior and its mechanism, while XOR provides an initial empirical test of previously speculative computational benefits. Correcting Equation (20) improves mathematical consistency. The overall gain is incremental: the central results were already supported, and the single XOR demonstration lacks important protocol details needed to assess and reproduce its broader implications.
